passage: Samir, you've been "fixing" that CV for three months, na? Let me tell you about your Reena mausi at twenty-one. I wanted to apply to a textile design studio in Ahmedabad. I spent the whole summer on my portfolio. Every sketch had to be perfect, or I tore it up. If one page was weak, the whole thing felt worthless. The deadline came, and I had four finished pages out of twenty. I didn't send it. The next year, the same. My friend Kokila sent a messy, half-ready portfolio and got in. I was so angry, mostly at myself. The third year I sent eight pages, not perfect, on time. They called me. Now go. Send yours tonight.

qa.q: How many pages had Reena finished by the first deadline?
qa.a: Reena had four finished pages out of twenty.

qa.q: How did Reena feel when Kokila got in with a messy portfolio?
qa.a: Reena felt angry, mostly about the choice not to send the portfolio.

qa.q: What turning point came in the third year?
qa.a: Reena sent eight imperfect pages on time instead of waiting for perfect, and the studio called Reena.

qa.q: What might Kokila's choice to send a messy, half-ready portfolio show about how Kokila saw deadlines?
qa.a: Kokila seems to have seen a deadline as a chance to be judged on real work, trusting that half-ready and sent beats perfect and unsent.

grounding: An aunt recalls how, at twenty-one, work had to be flawless or felt worthless, so deadlines passed until imperfect pages were finally sent.

passage: The application for the engineering trainee post closed at midnight, and the power had been out in the hostel since nine. Santosh sat in the corridor with his laptop at thirty percent, rewriting the first line of his cover letter for the twentieth time. "It has to be perfect or they'll bin it," he told Keerthana. "Otherwise it's pointless." He had skipped two other applications this month for the same reason. Keerthana watched the battery drop. "Is it good enough to send?" "It's... fine. But fine isn't enough." At eleven-forty the screen dimmed at ten percent. Santosh closed the laptop. "I'll wait for the next round." Keerthana said nothing, but she looked at him for a long moment.

qa.q: What time did the application close?
qa.a: It closed at midnight.

qa.q: What does Santosh's "fine isn't enough" suggest about how he thinks?
qa.a: It suggests he sees work as either perfect or worthless, so anything less feels pointless to send.

qa.q: What choice did Santosh make at eleven-forty, and what did it cost him?
qa.a: He closed the laptop and decided to wait, which meant another application went unsent.

qa.q: What might Keerthana be thinking as she looks at Santosh for a long moment?
qa.a: She may be worried and frustrated, watching Santosh let another good chance slip.

grounding: During a power cut before a deadline, a young man keeps rewriting because it must be flawless, and ends up not applying at all.

passage:
March: Gurpreet decided to apply for a design internship in Bengaluru. He opened the portfolio file, changed the font eleven times and closed it. "It has to be perfect, or they'll laugh," he told his sister, Gurleen.
April: The deadline passed. Gurpreet told everyone the internship wasn't worth it anyway. Secretly, he redid the cover page again.
May: Gurleen found a new deadline at a smaller studio and sat with him at the kitchen table. "Send the one you have. Not perfect. Just sent." His hands sweated over the button. He didn't press it that night. The next morning he did, and then felt sick for an hour.

qa.q: How many times did Gurpreet change the font?
qa.a: Eleven times.

qa.q: Why did Gurpreet say the internship wasn't worth it?
qa.a: He felt ashamed of missing the deadline and used the excuse to hide his fear of an imperfect portfolio.

qa.q: What helped Gurpreet finally send an application?
qa.a: Gurleen sitting with him and urging him to send what he had rather than wait for perfect.

qa.q: How might Gurleen feel watching him hesitate over the button?
qa.a: Gurleen likely feels patient but worried, wanting him to stop missing chances.

grounding: Shows a young adult who delays applying because the work isn't flawless, missing a deadline before finally sending.

passage: You think I was always this quick with letters? At twenty, beta, I couldn't finish anything. A scholarship form for a Delhi college sat in my drawer for three months because my handwriting on page two wasn't neat enough. Either it would be perfect, or I wouldn't send it at all. I missed that deadline. And the next one. My friend Deepak finally sat with me on our veranda with a pen and a clock. "One hour. Whatever's on the page, we post it." I, Devika, wept over one crooked line. We posted it. I didn't get that scholarship. But I got the next one, and I've sent a lot of imperfect letters since. Imperfect things get finished. Perfect ones stay in drawers.

qa.q: How long did the form sit in the drawer?
qa.a: For three months.

qa.q: What did young Devika feel over the crooked line?
qa.a: Devika felt upset and afraid, as if one flaw made the whole form worthless.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: Deepak sat with a pen and a clock and set one hour, so the form was finally posted.

qa.q: How might Deepak have felt watching the tears over one line?
qa.a: Deepak was probably patient and a little worried, determined to help the form finally get posted.

grounding: Shows a young adult caught in all-or-nothing thinking who misses deadlines until someone helps finish an imperfect form.

passage: The job portal closed at midnight, the hostel Wi-Fi kept dropping, and Rukmini still hadn't sent a single application. For three weeks she'd been polishing one cover letter. Every draft had something wrong: a stiff sentence, a word used twice. "If it's not perfect, they'll bin it anyway," she told Nazia, her roommate, who had already sent fourteen. At eleven the Wi-Fi died completely. Rukmini sat on the floor, surrounded by printed drafts, and felt the familiar mix of panic and relief: now she couldn't send it, so she couldn't fail. Nazia offered her phone's data. Rukmini stared at it. "It's not ready," she said. The clock turned midnight. Nothing was sent.

qa.q: How many applications had Nazia sent?
qa.a: Fourteen.

qa.q: What mix of feelings did Rukmini have when the Wi-Fi died?
qa.a: She felt panic and relief together, relieved that she couldn't send it and so couldn't fail.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could help next time?
qa.a: Waiting for a perfect letter meant nothing was sent; setting a time limit and sending a good-enough draft could help.

qa.q: What is it like for Nazia to offer her data and see it refused?
qa.a: Nazia may feel frustrated and worried for Rukmini, watching the deadline pass.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult whose all-or-nothing thinking leaves a job application unsent despite weeks of work.

passage:
The job portal on Arohi's laptop had been open for three weeks in their Chennai flat. Eleven saved listings. Zero applications.
"Did you send the design one?" Keerthana asked, dropping her bag.
"Not yet. My portfolio's not ready. The second project looks amateur."
"You've been saying that since March."
Arohi pulled her knees up. "If I send something average, they'll think I'm average. Then what's the point?"
"So it's perfect or nothing?"
"...Kind of."
Keerthana sat beside her and scrolled through the portfolio. "This is good. Not flawless. Good."
Arohi stared at the screen. The deadline for the design listing was midnight. Her cursor hovered over "Apply," then moved back to "Edit portfolio" again. She sighed, feeling stuck and tired of herself.

qa.q: How many listings had Arohi saved?
qa.a: Eleven.

qa.q: How does Arohi feel as her cursor moves back to "Edit portfolio"?
qa.a: She feels stuck and tired of herself, afraid that sending anything average means she is average.

qa.q: What small step could help Arohi get unstuck?
qa.a: She could send the design application tonight with the portfolio as it is, since Keerthana says it is good, and improve the second project later.

qa.q: How might Keerthana see Arohi's delay?
qa.a: Keerthana sees a good portfolio being held back since March and seems concerned, gently naming the perfect-or-nothing thinking.

grounding: Shows a young adult delaying job applications because her work may not be flawless, caught in all-or-nothing thinking.
